# The Lengthening Day

Somewhere in the Devonian, roughly 385 million years ago, a coral in a warm shallow sea laid down a thin band of calcium carbonate. It did the same the next day, and the next, as corals do. They grow a little faster in daylight than in darkness, so each day leaves a faint ridge. Over a year these ridges bunch and spread with the seasons, forming larger bands like tree rings, the annual pattern of warm and cool water written into stone.

In 1963, a paleontologist named John Wells counted those ridges on fossil corals. In modern corals he found about 360 fine lines per annual band, which is roughly what you'd expect from a creature marking the days of a 365-day year. The Devonian corals had around 400.

The year hasn't changed much. The Earth's orbit around the Sun takes about as long as it ever did. So if there were 400 days in a Devonian year, each day must have been shorter, about 22 hours. A coral that died before the first trees had finished colonizing the land was keeping a calendar, and its calendar says the world used to spin faster.

I want to write about this because it's one of my favorite facts, and because the longer I think about it the less it seems like a fact and the more it seems like a way of seeing.

---

The reason the day is lengthening is the Moon, and the reason the Moon matters is friction.

The Moon's gravity pulls on the Earth, and it pulls harder on the near side than on the far side. That difference stretches the planet slightly along the line between them, most visibly in the oceans, which bulge toward the Moon and away from it. Those are the tides. If the Earth didn't rotate, the bulges would simply sit there, pointing at the Moon, and nothing interesting would happen.

But the Earth does rotate, much faster than the Moon orbits, and it drags the bulges along with it. Water sloshing over continental shelves, grinding against coastlines, churning in shallow seas like the Bering Strait and the Patagonian shelf, can't keep perfect pace. The bulges end up carried slightly ahead of the line to the Moon. This misalignment works like a lever. The Moon's gravity tugs back on the leading bulge, applying a brake to the Earth's spin. Meanwhile the bulge's own gravity tugs forward on the Moon, feeding it energy and nudging it into a higher orbit.

So the Earth slows, and the Moon drifts away. Angular momentum that once lived in the Earth's spin is gradually handed over to the Moon's orbit. The total is conserved; it is just being moved from one account to another.

The rate is small but measurable. Apollo 11, 14, and 15 left arrays of corner-cube retroreflectors on the lunar surface, and two Soviet Lunokhod rovers carried them too. Observatories fire lasers at them, catch the handful of returning photons, and time the round trip. From decades of these measurements we know the Moon is receding at about 3.8 centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. The day, meanwhile, lengthens by something on the order of two milliseconds per century.

Two milliseconds a century sounds like nothing, and over a human life it is. But geology has time to spare. Two milliseconds a century is twenty seconds per million years, which is five and a half hours per billion. Run the clock backward far enough and you get the Devonian's 22-hour day, and further back still, days shorter than that.

---

What strikes me first is the quality of the evidence. Nobody set out to build an instrument for measuring the rotation of the ancient Earth. The instruments were already there, made by animals and sediments going about their business.

Corals are only one example. Certain ancient mollusks and brachiopods also laid down daily growth increments. Better still are tidal rhythmites, layered sediments deposited in estuaries and tidal flats, where each tide leaves a thin layer of silt and the thickness waxes and wanes with the monthly cycle of spring and neap tides. The Elatina Formation in South Australia, about 620 million years old, preserves such a record. Careful counting of its laminations has been used to estimate that the day then was a little under 22 hours and that there were about thirteen lunar months in a year.

There's something moving about this. A tidal flat on a planet with no animals larger than a few millimeters, mud settling in the dark, and hundreds of millions of years later someone with a hand lens counts the layers and recovers the length of a day no one experienced. The information was never lost. It was just waiting in a format nobody could read yet.

I think of this whenever someone says the past is gone. Much of it is, but a surprising amount is merely encoded, and the encoding is often more faithful than any human witness would have been.

---

The human witnesses are interesting too.

In 1695, Edmond Halley, comparing ancient eclipse records with the predictions of the lunar theory of his day, noticed that something didn't add up. The Moon seemed to be accelerating in its orbit relative to what the old observations implied. We now understand most of this apparent acceleration as an artifact: it isn't mainly that the Moon is speeding up but that our clock, the Earth's rotation, is slowing down. If you measure time by a clock that gradually runs slow, everything else seems to be speeding up.

In 1754, a young Immanuel Kant, decades before he became the philosopher of the *Critique of Pure Reason*, wrote a short essay on whether the Earth's rotation had changed since its origin. He argued, essentially correctly, that tidal friction must be slowing it and that the process would end with the Earth always turning the same face to the Moon. He couldn't quantify it, and he got some details wrong, but the core idea was right a century before anyone could measure it.

The most striking historical evidence comes from Babylon. Babylonian astronomers recorded eclipses on clay tablets with remarkable care: the date, the time, what was visible from where. If you take modern orbital mechanics, which gives the positions of the Sun and Moon precisely, and project back two and a half thousand years assuming the Earth has always rotated at today's rate, you can calculate where on the ground a given solar eclipse should have been visible. For many of the recorded eclipses the answer is wrong. The calculation puts the path of totality far to the west of Babylon, sometimes thousands of kilometers away, over places where no Babylonian was standing.

The eclipses happened where the tablets say they happened. What's wrong is the assumption of a constant spin. The accumulated difference between a uniformly rotating Earth and the real one, a quantity astronomers call ΔT, amounts to hours over that span. In effect, the planet has "lost" several hours of rotation since Nebuchadnezzar's time, relative to a perfect clock. The Babylonian scribes, recording what they saw with no idea of its significance, were measuring the braking of the world.

The researchers who did much of this work, notably F. Richard Stephenson and colleagues, found something else. The observed slowdown is a bit smaller than tidal friction alone would predict. Something is speeding the Earth up slightly. The main culprit seems to be the end of the last ice age. When the great ice sheets over North America and Scandinavia melted, the land beneath them, freed of its burden, began slowly rising, and it is still rising today. This redistributes mass toward the poles, like a figure skater drawing in her arms, and the Earth spins a little faster in response. The day we live in is the result of a tug-of-war between the Moon's patient drag and the Earth's slow recovery from glaciation.

---

This has practical consequences, which is where the story becomes almost comic.

For most of history, the second was defined as a fraction of the day. But by the mid-twentieth century atomic clocks had become so precise that the Earth itself was the least reliable clock in the room. So in 1967 the second was redefined in terms of the oscillations of cesium atoms: 9,192,631,770 of them. That created a problem. Atomic time ticks steadily; the Earth does not. Over years, the two drift apart.

The solution, adopted in 1972, was the leap second. Every so often, when the Earth fell far enough behind atomic time, an extra second was inserted, usually at the end of June or December, so that clocks read 23:59:60 before rolling over to midnight. Twenty-seven have been added since 1972.

Leap seconds are a nuisance for computers. Software that assumes every minute has sixty seconds can crash, and some notable outages have been blamed on them. There has been long argument about whether to keep them, and in 2022 the international body responsible voted to abandon them by 2035, allowing atomic time and Earth time to drift apart by larger amounts before any correction.

To complicate matters, in recent years the Earth has been spinning slightly faster than expected, for reasons involving the core, the atmosphere, and possibly melting ice, to the point where people seriously discussed the first-ever negative leap second. The long trend is toward slowing, but on short timescales the planet wobbles around it in ways that are still being untangled.

I love this. We built machines precise enough to catch the world being irregular. We had to decide, as a matter of international policy, how much we care whether noon happens when the Sun is highest. The ancient question of what time it is turns out to have two answers, one from atoms and one from the rotating rock we live on, and they don't agree.

---

Let me run the film backward all the way.

The leading theory for the Moon's origin is that, around 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth, and the Moon coalesced from the debris. If so, the early Moon formed very close, perhaps only a few tens of thousands of kilometers away, compared with about 384,000 today. It would have loomed enormous in the sky. The Earth was spinning very fast; a day may have been only a handful of hours. The tides, with the Moon so near, would have been immense, though what they would have looked like on a planet whose surface may have been largely molten is another question.

Since then the Moon has spiraled outward and the day has stretched, though not smoothly. One of the more intriguing ideas in this field is that for a long stretch of the Precambrian, perhaps a billion years, the length of the day may have stalled at around 19 hours. The proposed mechanism is atmospheric. The Sun heats the atmosphere on the day side, creating a thermal tide in the air itself, and this solar-driven tide pushes on the Earth's rotation in the opposite direction from the lunar tide. Normally it is much too weak to matter. But if the natural resonance of the atmosphere happened to line up with the length of the day, the solar push could have been amplified enough to balance the Moon's drag and hold the day steady for an immense stretch of time. This remains a hypothesis, supported by some geological evidence and disputed by some, but I find it beautiful: the air, warmed by sunlight, holding the planet's spin in place for a billion years, while below it the first complex cells were emerging.

Eventually the resonance broke, perhaps as the atmosphere's temperature changed, and the lengthening resumed. The Devonian coral, laying down its 400 bands a year, lived on the far side of that long pause.

---

And forward?

In principle, if nothing interfered, the process would continue until the Earth's rotation slowed to match the Moon's orbit, until one side of the Earth always faced the Moon just as one side of the Moon always faces us. The Moon would hang motionless in the sky over one hemisphere and never rise over the other. A day would last roughly as long as a month, which by then would be about 47 of our current days.

That won't actually happen. The timescale is tens of billions of years, and the Sun will swell into a red giant long before, in about five billion years. What becomes of the Earth then is uncertain, but it will not be a quiet tidal lock. Still, the direction of travel is clear. Every day is, by a tiny margin, the shortest of all the days to come.

---

Here is what I keep returning to.

We treat the day as the most basic unit of experience. It is the rhythm of sleep and waking, the framework of every schedule, the thing our bodies are built around. Our circadian clocks are tuned to a roughly 24-hour cycle, and every living thing on the surface has been shaped by alternating light and dark. It feels like the ground of time itself, the one thing that simply is what it is.

It isn't. It is a moving value, the current output of a long negotiation among the Earth's spin, the Moon's orbit, the friction of shallow seas, the weight of vanished ice, and perhaps the warmth of the air. The 24-hour day is a snapshot. The Devonian had its own; the far future will have another. The creatures of each era would have found theirs just as natural and unquestionable as we find ours.

I find this comforting rather than unsettling. It says the most stable-seeming features of the world are processes, not fixtures. They seem permanent only because they change slowly relative to us. The mountains are eroding, the continents are moving, the Moon is leaving at the speed of fingernails, and the day is getting longer, and none of this is a crisis. It is just what a world is: a set of slow motions that happen to look still from inside a human lifespan.

It also says something about attention. All of this was knowable, in principle, for a very long time. The coral bands were there. The tidal rhythmites were there. The Babylonian tablets were sitting in collections. What was missing was the frame that would make them legible, the idea that the day might have a history. Once someone asked the question, evidence appeared from everywhere: fossils, mud, clay, laser light bounced off mirrors left on the Moon by people who went there for entirely different reasons.

I suspect this is true of more things than we realize. Much of what we'd like to know is already recorded somewhere, in some material that has been faithfully keeping track while we weren't paying attention. The hard part is rarely gathering the data. It is thinking to ask.

---

Tonight the Moon will rise a little farther away than it did last night, by about a tenth of a millimeter. The day that ends will have been longer than a day in Babylon by a small fraction of a second. Somewhere a reef is laying down another thin band of carbonate, marking one more rotation of the Earth in a record no one will read for a very long time, if ever.

And the tides will come in, dragging very slightly ahead of the Moon, braking the world by an amount too small to feel, handing a little more of the Earth's momentum out into the dark. It has been happening the entire time you've been reading this. It was happening before there was anyone to read, and it will go on long after. I like knowing that. It makes the ordinary evening feel like part of something enormous and patient, which it is.
